name: Truncated cone
seoDesc: Truncated cone: work out volume from the slant height and the lateral surface area. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: volume is what the Truncated cone calculator works out, and it gets there from the slant height, the lateral surface area and the bottom surface area. It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Truncated cone calculator work?
sections.html:
The Truncated cone calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports volume in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the slant height (s), the lateral surface area and the bottom surface area.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Truncated cone calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Volume=(1 ÷ 3) × PI × height (h) × ((base radius (R) ^ 2) + base radius (R) × top radius (r) + (top radius (r) ^ 2))
Top radius (r)=lateral surface area ÷ (PI × slant height (s)) − base radius (R)
Height (h)=the square root of ((-base radius (R) + top radius (r) + slant height (s)) × (base radius (R) − top radius (r) + slant height (s)))
Total surface area=lateral surface area + PI × (base radius (R) ^ 2) + PI × (top radius (r) ^ 2)
Top surface area=PI × (top radius (r) ^ 2)
Base radius (R)=the square root of (bottom surface area) ÷ the square root of (PI)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic centimeters
  • Area, opening in square centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Truncated cone calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the slant height, the lateral surface area and the bottom surface area — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Truncated cone calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns volume, derived from the slant height, the lateral surface area and the bottom surface area. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Truncated cone calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the slant height, the lateral surface area and the bottom surface area, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height (h) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height (h) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Truncated cone calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
